title: Intraoperative fluorescence-guided fresh frozen sectioning for margin control in head and neck cancer: phase 2 clinical trial

paper_content.abstract:
Tumour-free margins (>5 mm) in head and neck malignancies improve prognosis, possibly impacting the need for
adjuvant treatment. In this phase II prospective, non-randomised trial (NCT05499065), we investigate the use of
fluorescence imaging using the tumour targeting fluorescent tracer cetuximab-IRDye800CW combined with fresh
frozen sectioning to identify inadequate margins intraoperatively in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma.
Primary objectives of our study are intraoperative detection of inadequate margins and additional resections, and
feasibility of implementing fluorescence-guided fresh frozen sectioning (FG-FFS) into the clinical workflow. In
this study, 10 out of 20 patients show inadequate margins after initial surgery; FG-FFS correctly classifies margin
in 19 patients. Additional resections increase tumour-free margin rates from 50% to 85%, where anatomical
boundaries limit further improvement in one patient. Intraoperative margin adjustment reduces the need for
adjuvant treatment in seven patients. These findings demonstrate that FG-FFS is a reliable and feasible method for
intraoperative margin assessment without delaying surgery.
paper_content.introduction:
Surgery is the primary treatment modality for many head and neck malignancies. Resection margins are considered
adequate when at least 5 mm wide.1–3 Despite this well-established requirement, tumour-free surgical margins are
achieved in only 30-65% of patients.4,5 Inadequate resections adversely impact survival and locoregional control:
five-year disease-free survival rates of approximately 79%, 63% and 52% for tumour-free (≥ 5 mm), close (< 5 mm
& ≥ 1 mm) and tumour-positive margins (< 1 mm), respectively.1–3,6,7
Call-back surgery for inadequate margin correction is challenging, as accurately relocating inadequate margins is
difficult, particularly in patients who have undergone reconstructive surgery.8 Achieving tumour-free margins at the
initial surgery is of major clinical importance, as adjuvant treatment cannot fully compensate for the negative
prognostic impact of initially inadequate margins.9,10
Fresh frozen sectioning (FFS) of the excised tumour specimen is the standard for evaluating margins during
surgery.11–14 An FFS procedure involves preparation of a 4 µm tissue section from a tissue slice, which has been
rapidly frozen after fresh sectioning using a cryostat. This frozen section is subsequently haematoxylin & eosin
(H&E) stained to assess tumour margins. Although intraoperative FFS provides a high specificity for margin
assessment, sampling error substantially reduces the sensitivity of this technique.15–18 Various approaches for
improved intraoperative identification of inadequate margins have been investigated.19,20 Fluorescence-guided
surgery using tumour targeted tracers has proven to be beneficial in head and neck cancer.21–25 The use of cetuximab-
IRDye800CW to detect oral cancer cells is feasible, since these cells overexpress epidermal growth factor
receptor.22 However, the intensity of the fluorescent signal does not reliably correlate with the margin width using
current fluorescence imaging approaches.25 To overcome this issue, a combined approach, supplementing
fluorescence imaging with intraoperative fresh frozen sectioning (i.e. fluorescence-guided fresh frozen sectioning
(FG-FFS)), has been developed. Although the combination of fluorescence imaging and fresh frozen sectioning has
been suggested previously, this has not been systematically investigated.23–25 Krishnan et al. examined the
localisation of fresh frozen sectioning based on clinical suspicion compared to a sentinel margin approach, which
uses the areas of highest fluorescence intensities as indicators of potentially inadequate margins. They found a
strong correlation between these approaches, however they did not investigate margins not suspected to be at risk.24
In this phase two intervention study, we demonstrate that fluorescence imaging of the whole resection specimen
and fresh tissue slices containing cetuximab-IRDye800CW successfully localizes margins at risk, while FFS
provides margin distance measurements of these margins in millimetres. This combined approach enables
fluorescence imaging to guide intraoperative pathology assessment beyond clinical suspicion alone, allowing for
timely recognition and intraoperative adjustment of inadequate margins.
paper_content.results:
The primary endpoints of this phase two study were the detection rates of inadequate margins by fluorescence
imaging only and FG-FFS, including the number of additional resection based on FG-FFS. Additionally, tracer
distribution (i.e. the spatial localisation of the cetuximab-800CW probe imaged with a fluorescence camera) was
evaluated and compared to pathology margins. Secondary endpoints for the study were patient characteristics and
feasibility of implementation and clinical application of FG-FFS into the current clinical workflow.

Patient and tumour characteristics
Between March 2023 and November 2024, 23 patients with histopathology proven oral squamous cell carcinoma
were included in this study. Study drugs consisting of unlabelled cetuximab and cetuximab-IRDye800CW were
administered intravenously two days prior to surgery. During study drug administration, two patients showed
infusion-related anaphylaxis to the unlabelled cetuximab, leading to termination of intravenous administration and
study exclusion. Both patients recovered after intramuscular adrenaline administration and an NaCl fluid challenge
and standard of care surgery could continue as scheduled. One other patient was excluded due to deviations from
the intraoperative imaging protocol, resulting in a total of 20 patients completing all study procedures. The
intraoperative FG-FFS margin assessment protocol is shown in Figure 1. An overview of the patient and tumour
characteristics is shown in Table 1 (secondary endpoint). The mean age of study participants was 57 (SD = 17.7),
13 (65%) patients were female. Tumours were primarily located in the tongue (n = 16) and staged pT1-3. Lymph
node metastases were present in four patients.

Surgical outcomes and clinical implication
Figure 1 gives an overview of the intraoperative specimen handling pipeline. Standard of care surgery resulted in
one tumour specimen per patient. This standard of care resection and subsequent pathology analysis, prior to any
study intervention, would have resulted in ten (50%) inadequate margins (Figure 2A). For study purposes, the whole
resection specimen was sliced into fresh tissue slices intraoperatively at the department of pathology of the
University Medical Centre Groningen (UMCG). The first primary endpoint of this study included the evaluation of
detection of inadequate margins by FG-FFS. FG-FFS based on the fresh tissue slices correctly identified margins
in 95% of patients (19 out of 20). One inadequate margin was missed where FG-FFS estimated a margin of 5.5
mm, but final pathology showed a margin of 4.5 mm. This resulted in a sensitivity, specificity and accuracy of
90.0%, 100.0% and 95.0%, respectively. Besides the identified closest margins by FG-FFS, no other locations with
inadequate margins were identified after complete pathology analysis.

Another primary endpoint was the immediate intraoperative additional resections that were performed in eight out
of nine patients with an inadequate margin identified by FG-FFS (Figure 2B). For one patient, anatomical
boundaries prevented an additional resection. The eight additional resections resulted in tumour-free margins at
final pathology assessment in seven patients (Figure 2C). Margins remained inadequate in one patient (Figure 2,
patient 9). In this case, the surgeon underestimated the additional resection width; a margin width of 1.1 mm was
converted into 3.3 mm. Overall, the final inadequate margin rate was reduced from 50% to 15%. Intraoperative
decision-making was performed within one hour (i.e. during treatment of the neck or preparations for reconstruction
of the defect) without delaying surgery and was therefore feasible within a clinical time-frame (secondary
endpoint).

Study related additional resections led to de-escalation or complete omission of margin-based adjuvant therapy in
seven of the ten patients who otherwise would have required therapy. Adjuvant therapy was entirely averted for
five patients, thereby preventing chemo-radiotherapy, radiotherapy or call-back surgery. For two patients, adjuvant
therapy was minimised to 56 Gy radiotherapy only instead of chemo-radiotherapy or 66 Gy radiotherapy (Figure
2A&C).

Correlation of FG-FFS margins with final pathology analysis
An important point to consider is whether the intraoperative margin provided by pathology based on FG-FFS is
comparable to the margin provided after final pathology analysis, when the tissue is formalin fixed and paraffin
embedded. In a retrospective analysis, these margin widths were compared. For this analysis, all patients with at
least one exact FFS margin in mm and final pathology margin width in mm of that same anatomical location, could
be included. Nineteen patients were included and one patient was excluded, due to a missing exact FFS margin
(recorded only to be greater than 5.1 mm). A significant difference (degrees of freedom (df) = 17, p < 0.001, effect
size = -1.07, 95% confidence interval (95% CI) = -1.16 – -0.43) was found between the FG-FFS margin estimate
and final pathology margin. Bland-Altman analysis revealed an average margin width overestimation of 0.8 mm
by FG-FFS, as shown in Figure 3. A post-hoc correction for this overestimation was performed to evaluate the
potential impact on this observed difference. After correcting FG-FFS margins for this overestimation, by
subtracting 0.8 mm from each determined FFS margin, no significant difference (df = 17, p = 0.591, effect size =
0.13, 95% CI = -0.25 – 0.43) remained between the FG-FFS margin and final pathology margin.

Analysis of other potential intraoperative assessment points
To further evaluate the first primary endpoint, data of other potential intraoperative assessment points other than
fresh tissue slice FG-FFS were separately analysed. These points included fluorescence imaging only of the whole
resection specimen, fluorescence imaging only of the fresh tissue slices and whole resection specimen FG-FFS.
Note that these assessment points were all performed for every resection as the steps did not interfere with one
another. As shown in Figure 1, fluorescence imaging of the whole resection specimen was performed first, followed
by identification of spots and demarcation with a needle (‘fluorescence imaging only of the whole resection
specimen’ in Table 2). Next, the specimen was cut into fresh tissue slices, followed by imaging of these tissue slices
(fluorescence imaging only of fresh tissue slices) to identify tissue slices with potential inadequate margins. For
whole resection specimen FG-FFS, an FFS of the tissue slice with the demarcation needle was acquired; for fresh
tissue slice FG-FFS, an FFS of the tissue slice with the estimated closest margin was acquired. Sensitivity,
specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) for all four strategies are
shown in Table 2. The endpoint tracer distribution and its correlation to final histopathology, was assessed using
fluorescence imaging of the whole resection specimen. Fluorescence imaging only of the whole resection specimen
analysis (Figure 1.2) accurately identified tumour-positive margins (< 1 mm), as all four detected spots (spot-to-
background ratios (SBRs) ranging between 1.7 and 2.1) were tumour-positive. However, absence of a spot was not
indicative for tumour-free margins (> 5 mm), as shown by the low sensitivity caused by six false negative cases.
Contrarily, fluorescence imaging only of the fresh tissue slices (Figure 1.4) was indicative for tumour-free margins,
but did show seven false inadequate margins. During fresh tissue slice FG-FFS, these false inadequate margins
were corrected by FFS, increasing specificity. Representative examples of inadequate and tumour-free resection
margins are shown in Figure 4.
paper_content.methods:
Study design and participants
A phase two, non-randomized, non-blinded, prospective, and interventional study was performed at the
department of Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery of the UMCG, the Netherlands. The Institutional Review Board of the
UMCG approved the study (METc 2022/456) and it was conducted according to the Dutch Act on Medical Research
involving Human Subjects (WMO) and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki (adapted version of Fortaleza,
Brazil, 2013). The study is registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05499065).
Patients ≥18 years old with histopathology proven oral squamous cell carcinoma scheduled to undergo surgery, as
decided in the multidisciplinary head and neck tumour board meeting of the UMCG, were eligible for inclusion in
the study. All eligible patients were included regardless of sex or gender. Sex was registered for baseline
characteristics using electronical patient record data documented in the hospital electronic patient records, as self-
reported by each patient. After obtaining written informed consent, inclusion and exclusion criteria were checked.
Briefly, patients were included if they showed no evidence of QTc prolongation, were not pregnant or lactating,
and had no history of allergy or infusion reactions to monoclonal antibodies.

Fluorescent tracer administration
The study drug cetuximab-IRDye800CW was produced under Good Manufacturing Practice in the UMCG, and
released by a qualified person.39 Two days before surgery, study drugs were administered intravenously in
accordance with the previously published tracer administration protocol.22,25 First, an intravenous dose of 2 mg
clemastine was given, according to standard of care cetuximab treatment to reduce allergic reaction risk. Next,
patients received 75 mg unlabelled cetuximab as a pre-dose, followed by 15 mg fluorescently labelled cetuximab,
cetuximab-IRDye800CW, after one hour. Pre-dosing using unlabelled cetuximab improves fluorescent tracer
localization in the tumour, as shown previously.22

Intraoperative margin assessment
An overview of the intraoperative margin assessment protocol is shown in Figure 1. Surgery started with primary
tumour resection, followed by treatment of the neck. During tumour resection, paired tagging was performed for
orientation purposes. Paired tagging consists of stitches marked with clips placed in the mucosa of both the surgical
cavity and the resection specimen on at least four corresponding anatomical locations. Stiches at matching
anatomical locations were marked with the same number of clips. Paired tagging ensured accurate relocation of the
anatomical site within the surgical cavity in case of an inadequate margin (Figure 1.1).16 In this study, in-vivo
imaging was not performed, since this results in inadequate illumination of the resection margins and therefore
limits assessment. Imaging of the excised specimen is more straightforward, enabling proper and standardised
illumination of all surgical margins. Ex-vivo fluorescence imaging therefore served as red flag technique for fresh
frozen sectioning.36
Immediately after tumour excision, all sides of the resected specimen were imaged using a closed-field fluorescence
camera (i.e. PEARL-trilogy®, LI-COR BioSciences Inc., Lincoln, NE, USA) at the department of Pathology and
Medical Biology of the UMCG. The acquired images were scaled relative to the maximum intensity of the
tumour/mucosal side using ImageJ (version 1.53t, Fiji, Bethesda, MD, USA). Subsequently, two observers assessed
the images for fluorescent spots using the colormap MPL-inferno, indicating possible inadequate margins. When
a spot was identified, an SBR was calculated using formula (1):
SBR = I_spot / I_background (1)
with I being the mean intensity. The background region of interest was identified on the same image as the spot,
based on all tissue adjacent to the spot of a similar origin (e.g. muscle, fat) and identical distance to the camera (as
shown in Figure 4A). A spot with an SBR > 1.5 was marked on the whole resection specimen using a needle,
followed by a fluorescence image to confirm the marker location. The location of this needle served as the reference
for whole resection specimen FG-FFS, as shown in Figure 1.
Subsequently, the resection sides of the specimen were inked, and the specimen was freshly cut into 3 - 5 mm thick
tissue slices by dedicated pathology staff. Next, images of all fresh tissue slices were acquired using the
fluorescence camera. Delineation of tumour tissue on fluorescence images was performed by two observers, based
on maximum fluorescence intensity and a substantial drop-off of signal towards all resection sides. From these
estimated tumour outlines, resection margins were measured on the images of the tissue slices, identifying the
closest margins based on fluorescence imaging. In case of disagreement between observers, a third observer was
consulted. If, based on fluorescence imaging, all margins were assessed as being tumour-free, FFS was performed
of the fresh tissue slice containing the estimated closest margin. When one or more inadequate margin(s) were
suspected based on fluorescence imaging of the fresh tissue slices, FFS of these margins was performed. In case
FFS confirmed an inadequate margin, the surgeon was informed by the pathologist. An additional resection was
performed if deemed clinically feasible and safe. Determining the exact location for additional resection was
essential for effective treatment. To ensure this, the following measures were taken: continuous orientation tracking
by two dedicated researchers throughout tissue imaging and processing, paired tagging to preserve anatomical
orientation, documentation of cutting planes during tissue slicing to enable accurate relocation of tissue slices in
the original resection specimen, and collaborative reporting by pathologist and researchers to the surgeon of the
precise location of any inadequate margins identified in the FFS. An exemption to this workflow was made only
for cases in which a tumour-positive margin was apparent based on visual and tactile assessment by both pathologist
and surgeon and fluorescence imaging of the fresh tissue slices. Even though not proven by FFS, an immediate
additional resection was performed. Altogether, two FG-FFS methods were investigated: 1) FFS of the tissue slice
identified by a spot and marked with a needle on whole resection specimen fluorescence imaging, and 2) FFS of
the tissue slice identified as the slice containing the closest margin by fresh tissue slice fluorescence imaging.
Following the FFS procedure, the fresh tissue slices were formalin fixed for at least 24h, followed by paraffin
embedding and 4 µm sectioning for H&E staining, according to standard of care. Based on the standard of care
H&E staining assessment, margins before and after potential additional resections were assessed by a pathologist.
Based on pathology results before and after study intervention, adjuvant treatment was determined by the
multidisciplinary head and neck tumour board of the UMCG. During the trial, adverse events were reported to the
Institutional Review Board using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 6.0.

Endpoints
In this study, three primary and two secondary endpoints were evaluated. The first primary endpoint was the
comparison between fluorescence imaging alone and FG-FFS for detecting tumour-positive and close surgical
margins. Diagnostic accuracy was evaluated by calculating sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, PPV and NPV for both
methods. An additional primary endpoint was the number of additional resections performed based on FG-FFS data
and the corresponding postoperative pathology outcomes. Tracer distribution, evaluated by correlating SBR values
of the whole resection specimen with margin widths, and conversely, margin widths with SBR values, was the last
primary endpoint of this study. The secondary endpoints were patient characteristics, feasibility of on-site
intraoperative tissue analysis by the surgeon and pathologist and feasibility of novel 3D imaging methods of the
obtained additional biopsies. Feasibility of novel 3D imaging methods of the obtained additional biopsies is not
reported here as it did not align with the primary focus of the trial. Feasibility of the analysis was assessed based
on duration of surgical procedures and integration of FG-FFS into the operative workflow.

Statistics & Reproducibility
The sample size was calculated using a two-proportion power analysis, assuming a baseline proportion of 0.5, an
expected proportion of 0.2, a 95% confidence level, 80% power, and resulted in a required sample size of at least
19 patients. Patients were excluded from the analysis in case they did not undergo all study procedures. The patients
were not randomised.
Descriptive statistics of patient demographics were tested using the Anderson-Darling test, D’Agostino & Pearson
test, Shapiro-Wilk test and Kolmogorov-Smirnov test using GraphPad Prism (version 9.0, GraphPad Software Inc,
San Diego, California, USA). Normally distributed data were reported using mean with standard deviation (SD)
and non-gaussian data using the median with interquartile range (IQR). Next, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, PPV
and NPV for margin assessment were calculated for both fluorescence imaging only and FG-FFS. Finally, FG-FFS
margin widths were compared with final pathology margins using a paired t-test and Bland-Altman analysis to
assess a potential bias. As this manuscript concerns a clinical intervention trial, all experiments could only be
performed once (during surgery).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Summary: The manuscript is a phase II clinical trial in surgical treatment of oral cancer using tumor targeted fluorescence
guidance using cetuximab-IRDye800CW in the assessment of intra-operative margin detection and its clinical applicability.
The primary end points of the study were detection of inadequate margin rates, additional resections and their clinical
implications. Secondary endpoints assessed the feasibility of FG-FFS implementation into current SOC workflows were
discussed.
Primary outcomes were as follows: Out of the 20 patients included in the study, 50% (10) patients had inadequate margins,
8/9 patients among these underwent additional resections, 7/8 of these patients showed tumor free margins at final
pathological assessment. Overall, the final inadequate margin rate was reduced from 50% to 15%. The FG-FFS based on
fresh tissue slices identified margins in 95% (19 out 20) patients.
Secondary outcomes showed that FG-FFS was feasible within a clinical-time frame. The additional resections led to de-
escalation or complete omission of margin-based adjuvant therapy in 7/10 patients who would otherwise have required
therapy. Out of these 7 patients, adjuvant therapy, entirely averted in 5 patients, and reduced in 2 patients.
Authors and the findings of the study make a strong case of incorporating fluorescence guidance into SOC surgical
workflows which can lead to better outcomes compared to the current methods. Review of the manuscript raised the
following points and comments for the authors to consider.
Specific comments to be addressed:
1. Additional methodology clarity is needed for the whole tumor specimen FG-FFS. Was a shaving made from the whole
specimen for frozen section analysis prior to cutting the whole tumor into 3-5mm sections? Or did the final FG-FFS tissue
section serve as a comparator for the whole tumor specimen as well as for the fresh tissue slice identified by fluorescence?
2. Please clarify if only one tissue per patient was used to evaluate close/positive margins via fluorescence (whole
specimen, fresh tissue, FG-FFS), and confirm whether pathology showed no additional close/positive margins in other tissue
specimens NOT used for FG-FFS. (The latter was not clear based on the results/methods.)
3. Please clarify how correction was made for overestimation of margin width by FG-FFS relative to pathology; does this
mean that tissues showing overestimation of margin width were excluded from the subsequent comparison? If so, how many
tissues remained for comparison?
4. Table 2: what is the difference between FG-FFS in whole resection specimen vs FG-FFS in fresh tissue splice? Please
clarify in the methods.
5. Table 2: needs further clarification on fluorescence imaging only and fluorescence-guided fresh frozen sectioning. What is
meant by each must be defined.
6. Table 1: please include patient specific DOI and staging for each case, rather than a consolidated data. Deep margin
status for each case, if available.
7. How was orientation between the whole specimen and the fresh frozen samples maintained during fluorescence
imaging? Is there a possibility of sampling error? Could the corrected overestimation of 0.8mm during fluorescence be
relative to the patient and tumor characteristics?
8. Defining the terms like Fresh-frozen slice, tracer distribution, and fluorescence-imaging only, would be helpful.
9. Please specify in abstract that the study is phase II prospective non randomized.
10. Define parallel tagging (page 7, 11) for readers outside surgical oncology
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Comments for authors:
1. The authors are to be congratulated on a novel approach to improving oncologically sound surgical resections.
2. In the abstract. The statement “ necessitate additional therapy to reduce recurrence risk.” Is probably overly optimistic
concerning the assumption that additional therapy reduces risk following an oncologically unsound resection.
3. The fact that up to 85% of SOC surgery leads to inadequate margins is a surprisingly high percentage. Is this an unusual
patient population in the Netherlands or is “ inadequate margin” being defined in a different way, or is this group of surgeons’
experience with positive margins different from the typical rates?
4. Under results, it would be helpful to explicitly define “ inadequate margin detection”
5. How were the 23 patients selected for this study? In a center that no doubt sees many more than 23 OCSCC patients in
20 months, this suggests the possibility of a selection bias.
6. The patient population consisted of 65% female . This is a very unusual sex distribution.
7. The statement “but final pathology showed a margin of 4.5 mm.” could use some clarification. It is understood that there
was FG- FFS done on fresh tissue slices at the time of the operation to determine fluorescence based margins, but was the
final pathological margin status also incorporating fluorescence on the final preserved samples? That is, doing fluorescence
evaluation on the final path specimens might change the “ gold standard” of routine H and E pathology for final margin
adequacy .
8. With the recent data concerning presurgical treatment of advanced OCSCC with ICI, do the authors want to comment on
the challenges of applying these data to this new sequential treatment paradigm?
9. The statement that “ clinical implementation was uncomplicated” is perhaps too tunnel- visioned a focus on surgical time.
Surely cetuximab related anaphylaxis in 2/23 patients should be considered somewhat complicated.
10. Many of the statements throughout the manuscript seem to suggest a known benefit in terms of fluorescence – based
margin assessment and reduction in adjuvant treatment and therefore reduced relapses and toxicity. This is a very forward
leaning assumption that cannot be validated by small datasets from uncontrolled trials. The notion that “increase in correct
intraoperative margin assessment “ is an end goal in itself can only be made if an appropriately designed trial, likely with a
control arm, demonstrates that a clinically relevant outcome like OS, PFS, morbidity is both clinically and statistically
significantly changed. The assumption that the omission or reduction in 70% of margin – based treatment did not
compromise clinically relevant endpoints is speculative, A tumor board endorsement of such reductions does not change the
speculative nature of this statement.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Dear Editor,
Hereby, we would like to thank you and the reviewers for your time and the decision to
invite us to revise our work based on the reviewers’ comments. Below, our response to the
reviewers is provided. First, we focused on the overall comments of the reviewer, and
subsequently responded to their detailed comments on a point-by-point basis. Besides,
the requested formatting instructions and editorial policies were addressed. The changes
made to our manuscript are highlighted in red. In the attachments, you can find two
versions of the adapted manuscript, one with, and one without highlighted changes for
your convenience.
Reviewer #1
Overall, the reviewer elegantly summarizes our study and the main findings. We are
grateful that the reviewer recognizes the strong case of incorporating fluorescence
guidance into SOC surgical workflows, which can lead to better outcomes compared to
the current methods.
On a point-by-point basis the reviewer’s detailed comments have been addressed below:
1. Additional methodology clarity is needed for the whole tumour specimen FG-FFS.
Was a shaving made from the whole specimen for frozen section analysis prior to
cutting the whole tumour into 3-5mm sections? Or did the final FG-FFS tissue
section serve as a comparator for the whole tumour specimen as well as for the fresh
tissue slice identified by fluorescence?
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this unclarity in the methodology.
The whole resection specimen was ex vivo imaged for fluorescent spots. If there were
any present these fluorescent spots were marked with a needle. Subsequently, the
resection specimen was cut into 3-5 mm tissue slices with this needle still in place.
There were no shavings taken from the margins, the whole specimen was cut in
slices. A fresh frozen section of the tissue slice containing the needle was obtained
and therefore served as the final FG-FFS outcome for whole resection specimen FG-
FFS. Subsequently, fluorescence images of the tissue slices were obtained to
estimate the closest margin based on fluorescence analysis of these slices. FFS of
the tissue slice with the estimated closest margin based on fluorescence imaging
served as the final FG-FFS outcome for fresh tissue slice FG-FFS. It should be noted
that the tissue slice identified by whole resection specimen fluorescence imaging
could therefore differ from the tissue slice identified based on the fresh tissue slice
fluorescence imaging. In summary: The decision where to obtain tissue for an FFS
was determined in two different stages of the pathology analysis (see figure for visual
representation):
1) The tissue slice for whole resection specimen FG-FFS was identified by whole
resection specimen fluorescence imaging and marked with a needle;
2) The tissue slice for fresh tissue slice FG-FFS was identified based on fresh tissue
slice fluorescence imaging.
Figure: Visual representation of the difference between whole resection specimen FG-FFS and fresh
tissue slice FG-FFS within the same study patient. Whole resection specimen FG-FFS is based only
on whole specimen fluorescence imaging, whereas fresh tissue slice FG-FFS is based on the
fluorescence images of fresh tissue slices.
To clarify the methodology, we have made the following changes to the manuscript
and have adjusted our figure 1 to clarify the differences between the two techniques:
• Manuscript pages 5-6, paragraph 5 (‘In-depth analysis of other potential
intraoperative assessment points’): These points included fluorescence imaging
only of the whole resection specimen, fluorescence imaging only of the fresh
tissue slices and whole resection specimen FG-FFS. Note that these assessment
points were all performed for every resection as the steps did not interfere with one
another. As shown in Figure 1, fluorescence imaging of the whole resection
specimen was performed first, followed by identification of spots and
demarcation with a needle (‘fluorescence imaging only of the whole resection
specimen’ in Table 2). Next, the specimen was cut into fresh tissue slices, followed
by imaging of these tissue slices (fluorescence imaging only of fresh tissue slices)
to identify tissue slices with potential inadequate margins. For whole resection
specimen FG-FFS, an FFS of the tissue slice with the demarcation needle was
acquired; for fresh tissue slice FG-FFS, an FFS of the tissue slice with the
estimated closest margin was acquired.
• Manuscript page 10, paragraph 1: A spot with an SBR > 1.5 was marked on the
whole resection specimen using a needle, followed by a fluorescence image to
confirm the marker location. The location of this needle served as the reference
for whole resection specimen FG-FFS, as shown in Figure 1.
• Manuscript page 10, paragraph 2: Even though not proven by FFS, an immediate
additional resection was performed. Altogether, two FG-FFS methods were
investigated: 1) FFS of the tissue slice identified by a spot and marked with a
needle on whole resection specimen fluorescence imaging, and 2) FFS of the
tissue slice identified as the slice containing the closest margin by fresh tissue
slice fluorescence imaging.
• Manuscript Figure 1: This figure was adapted to provide a clear overview of the
study procedures, while also providing a clear distinction between whole tissue
specimen FG-FFS and fresh tissue slice FG-FFS approaches.
2. Please clarify if only one tissue per patient was used to evaluate close/positive
margins via fluorescence (whole specimen, fresh tissue, FG-FFS), and confirm
whether pathology showed no additional close/positive margins in other tissue
specimens NOT used for FG-FFS. (The latter was not clear based on the
results/methods.)
Response: In this study, only one whole resection specimen was used per patient.
Each specimen was evaluated using the proposed 1) whole resection specimen FG-
FFS and 2) fresh tissue slice FG-FFS workflows, as we clarified in our response to the
reviewer’s previous comment (reviewer 1, comment 1). In these specimens, the
anatomical location of the closest margin was correctly identified using fresh tissue
slice FG-FFS. In 19 of the 20 patients, the margin status (i.e. inadequate (≤ 5mm) or
free (> 5 mm)) always corresponded to final histopathology. In one patient, FG-FFS
deemed the margin to be free, but final pathology showed an inadequate margin (4.5
mm). No other inadequate margins were found on other anatomical locations in
these specimens by final pathology analysis.
To prevent any misunderstanding, we have revised the manuscript as follows:
• Manuscript, page 5, paragraph 1 (‘Surgical outcomes and clinical implication
of intraoperative FG-FFS decision making’): Figure 1 gives an overview of the
intraoperative specimen handling pipeline. Standard of care surgery resulted in
one tumour specimen per patient. This standard of care regular surgical resection
and subsequent pathology analysis, prior to any study intervention, would have
resulted in ten (50%) inadequate margins (Figure 2A).
• Manuscript, page 5, paragraph 1 (‘Surgical outcomes and clinical implication
of intraoperative FG-FFS decision making’): This resulted in a sensitivity,
specificity and accuracy of 90.0%, 100.0% and 95.0%, respectively. Besides the
identified closest margins by FG-FFS, no other locations with inadequate margins
were identified after complete pathology analysis.
3. Please clarify how correction was made for overestimation of margin width by FG-
FFS relative to pathology; does this mean that tissues showing overestimation of
margin width were excluded from the subsequent comparison? If so, how many
tissues remained for comparison?
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity in the interpretation
of the margin overestimation by FG-FFS. The intraoperative margins were
determined on H&E stained fresh frozen sections and compared to formalin fixed
final H&E histopathology and thus could only be compared after all study procedures
were completed. For the margin comparison itself, all patients with a known

## Abstract

Tumour-free margins (>5 mm) in head and neck malignancies improve prognosis, possibly impacting the need for
adjuvant treatment. In this phase II prospective, non-randomised trial (NCT05499065), we investigate the use of
fluorescence imaging using the tumour targeting fluorescent tracer cetuximab-IRDye800CW combined with fresh
frozen sectioning to identify inadequate margins intraoperatively in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma.
Primary objectives of our study are intraoperative detection of inadequate margins and additional resections, and
feasibility of implementing fluorescence-guided fresh frozen sectioning (FG-FFS) into the clinical workflow. In
this study, 10 out of 20 patients show inadequate margins after initial surgery; FG-FFS correctly classifies margin
in 19 patients. Additional resections increase tumour-free margin rates from 50% to 85%, where anatomical
boundaries limit further improvement in one patient. Intraoperative margin adjustment reduces the need for
adjuvant treatment in seven patients. These findings demonstrate that FG-FFS is a reliable and feasible method for
intraoperative margin assessment without delaying surgery.

---

## Introduction

Surgery is the primary treatment modality for many head and neck malignancies. Resection margins are considered
adequate when at least 5 mm wide.1–3 Despite this well-established requirement, tumour-free surgical margins are
achieved in only 30-65% of patients.4,5 Inadequate resections adversely impact survival and locoregional control:
five-year disease-free survival rates of approximately 79%, 63% and 52% for tumour-free (≥ 5 mm), close (< 5 mm
& ≥ 1 mm) and tumour-positive margins (< 1 mm), respectively.1–3,6,7
Call-back surgery for inadequate margin correction is challenging, as accurately relocating inadequate margins is
difficult, particularly in patients who have undergone reconstructive surgery.8 Achieving tumour-free margins at the
initial surgery is of major clinical importance, as adjuvant treatment cannot fully compensate for the negative
prognostic impact of initially inadequate margins.9,10
Fresh frozen sectioning (FFS) of the excised tumour specimen is the standard for evaluating margins during
surgery.11–14 An FFS procedure involves preparation of a 4 µm tissue section from a tissue slice, which has been
rapidly frozen after fresh sectioning using a cryostat. This frozen section is subsequently haematoxylin & eosin
(H&E) stained to assess tumour margins. Although intraoperative FFS provides a high specificity for margin
assessment, sampling error substantially reduces the sensitivity of this technique.15–18 Various approaches for
improved intraoperative identification of inadequate margins have been investigated.19,20 Fluorescence-guided
surgery using tumour targeted tracers has proven to be beneficial in head and neck cancer.21–25 The use of cetuximab-
IRDye800CW to detect oral cancer cells is feasible, since these cells overexpress epidermal growth factor
receptor.22 However, the intensity of the fluorescent signal does not reliably correlate with the margin width using
current fluorescence imaging approaches.25 To overcome this issue, a combined approach, supplementing
fluorescence imaging with intraoperative fresh frozen sectioning (i.e. fluorescence-guided fresh frozen sectioning
(FG-FFS)), has been developed. Although the combination of fluorescence imaging and fresh frozen sectioning has
been suggested previously, this has not been systematically investigated.23–25 Krishnan et al. examined the
localisation of fresh frozen sectioning based on clinical suspicion compared to a sentinel margin approach, which
uses the areas of highest fluorescence intensities as indicators of potentially inadequate margins. They found a
strong correlation between these approaches, however they did not investigate margins not suspected to be at risk.24
In this phase two intervention study, we demonstrate that fluorescence imaging of the whole resection specimen
and fresh tissue slices containing cetuximab-IRDye800CW successfully localizes margins at risk, while FFS
provides margin distance measurements of these margins in millimetres. This combined approach enables
fluorescence imaging to guide intraoperative pathology assessment beyond clinical suspicion alone, allowing for
timely recognition and intraoperative adjustment of inadequate margins.

---

## Results

The primary endpoints of this phase two study were the detection rates of inadequate margins by fluorescence
imaging only and FG-FFS, including the number of additional resection based on FG-FFS. Additionally, tracer
distribution (i.e. the spatial localisation of the cetuximab-800CW probe imaged with a fluorescence camera) was
evaluated and compared to pathology margins. Secondary endpoints for the study were patient characteristics and
feasibility of implementation and clinical application of FG-FFS into the current clinical workflow.

Patient and tumour characteristics
Between March 2023 and November 2024, 23 patients with histopathology proven oral squamous cell carcinoma
were included in this study. Study drugs consisting of unlabelled cetuximab and cetuximab-IRDye800CW were
administered intravenously two days prior to surgery. During study drug administration, two patients showed
infusion-related anaphylaxis to the unlabelled cetuximab, leading to termination of intravenous administration and
study exclusion. Both patients recovered after intramuscular adrenaline administration and an NaCl fluid challenge
and standard of care surgery could continue as scheduled. One other patient was excluded due to deviations from
the intraoperative imaging protocol, resulting in a total of 20 patients completing all study procedures. The
intraoperative FG-FFS margin assessment protocol is shown in Figure 1. An overview of the patient and tumour
characteristics is shown in Table 1 (secondary endpoint). The mean age of study participants was 57 (SD = 17.7),
13 (65%) patients were female. Tumours were primarily located in the tongue (n = 16) and staged pT1-3. Lymph
node metastases were present in four patients.

Surgical outcomes and clinical implication
Figure 1 gives an overview of the intraoperative specimen handling pipeline. Standard of care surgery resulted in
one tumour specimen per patient. This standard of care resection and subsequent pathology analysis, prior to any
study intervention, would have resulted in ten (50%) inadequate margins (Figure 2A). For study purposes, the whole
resection specimen was sliced into fresh tissue slices intraoperatively at the department of pathology of the
University Medical Centre Groningen (UMCG). The first primary endpoint of this study included the evaluation of
detection of inadequate margins by FG-FFS. FG-FFS based on the fresh tissue slices correctly identified margins
in 95% of patients (19 out of 20). One inadequate margin was missed where FG-FFS estimated a margin of 5.5
mm, but final pathology showed a margin of 4.5 mm. This resulted in a sensitivity, specificity and accuracy of
90.0%, 100.0% and 95.0%, respectively. Besides the identified closest margins by FG-FFS, no other locations with
inadequate margins were identified after complete pathology analysis.

Another primary endpoint was the immediate intraoperative additional resections that were performed in eight out
of nine patients with an inadequate margin identified by FG-FFS (Figure 2B). For one patient, anatomical
boundaries prevented an additional resection. The eight additional resections resulted in tumour-free margins at
final pathology assessment in seven patients (Figure 2C). Margins remained inadequate in one patient (Figure 2,
patient 9). In this case, the surgeon underestimated the additional resection width; a margin width of 1.1 mm was
converted into 3.3 mm. Overall, the final inadequate margin rate was reduced from 50% to 15%. Intraoperative
decision-making was performed within one hour (i.e. during treatment of the neck or preparations for reconstruction
of the defect) without delaying surgery and was therefore feasible within a clinical time-frame (secondary
endpoint).

Study related additional resections led to de-escalation or complete omission of margin-based adjuvant therapy in
seven of the ten patients who otherwise would have required therapy. Adjuvant therapy was entirely averted for
five patients, thereby preventing chemo-radiotherapy, radiotherapy or call-back surgery. For two patients, adjuvant
therapy was minimised to 56 Gy radiotherapy only instead of chemo-radiotherapy or 66 Gy radiotherapy (Figure
2A&C).

Correlation of FG-FFS margins with final pathology analysis
An important point to consider is whether the intraoperative margin provided by pathology based on FG-FFS is
comparable to the margin provided after final pathology analysis, when the tissue is formalin fixed and paraffin
embedded. In a retrospective analysis, these margin widths were compared. For this analysis, all patients with at
least one exact FFS margin in mm and final pathology margin width in mm of that same anatomical location, could
be included. Nineteen patients were included and one patient was excluded, due to a missing exact FFS margin
(recorded only to be greater than 5.1 mm). A significant difference (degrees of freedom (df) = 17, p < 0.001, effect

and final pathology margin. Bland-Altman analysis revealed an average margin width overestimation of 0.8 mm

potential impact on this observed difference. After correcting FG-FFS margins for this overestimation, by

0.13, 95% CI = -0.25 – 0.43) remained between the FG-FFS margin and final pathology margin.

To further evaluate the first primary endpoint, data of other potential intraoperative assessment points other than

resection specimen, fluorescence imaging only of the fresh tissue slices and whole resection specimen FG-FFS.
Note that these assessment points were all performed for every resection as the steps did not interfere with one
another. As shown in Figure 1, fluorescence imaging of the whole resection specimen was performed first, followed
by identification of spots and demarcation with a needle (‘fluorescence imaging only of the whole resection
specimen’ in Table 2). Next, the specimen was cut into fresh tissue slices, followed by imaging of these tissue slices

shown in Table 2. The endpoint tracer distribution and its correlation to final histopathology, was assessed using
fluorescence imaging of the whole resection specimen. Fluorescence imaging only of the whole resection specimen
analysis (Figure 1.2) accurately identified tumour-positive margins (< 1 mm), as all four detected spots (spot-to-
background ratios (SBRs) ranging between 1.7 and 2.1) were tumour-positive. However, absence of a spot was not
indicative for tumour-free margins (> 5 mm), as shown by the low sensitivity caused by six false negative cases.
Contrarily, fluorescence imaging only of the fresh tissue slices (Figure 1.4) was indicative for tumour-free margins,

## Methods

Study design and participants
A phase two, non-randomized, non-blinded, prospective, and interventional study was performed at the
department of Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery of the UMCG, the Netherlands. The Institutional Review Board of the
UMCG approved the study (METc 2022/456) and it was conducted according to the Dutch Act on Medical Research
involving Human Subjects (WMO) and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki (adapted version of Fortaleza,
Brazil, 2013). The study is registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05499065).
Patients ≥18 years old with histopathology proven oral squamous cell carcinoma scheduled to undergo surgery, as
decided in the multidisciplinary head and neck tumour board meeting of the UMCG, were eligible for inclusion in
the study. All eligible patients were included regardless of sex or gender. Sex was registered for baseline
characteristics using electronical patient record data documented in the hospital electronic patient records, as self-

Briefly, patients were included if they showed no evidence of QTc prolongation, were not pregnant or lactating,
and had no history of allergy or infusion reactions to monoclonal antibodies.

Fluorescent tracer administration
The study drug cetuximab-IRDye800CW was produced under Good Manufacturing Practice in the UMCG, and
released by a qualified person.39 Two days before surgery, study drugs were administered intravenously in
accordance with the previously published tracer administration protocol.22,25 First, an intravenous dose of 2 mg
clemastine was given, according to standard of care cetuximab treatment to reduce allergic reaction risk. Next,
patients received 75 mg unlabelled cetuximab as a pre-dose, followed by 15 mg fluorescently labelled cetuximab,

localization in the tumour, as shown previously.22

An overview of the intraoperative margin assessment protocol is shown in Figure 1. Surgery started with primary
tumour resection, followed by treatment of the neck. During tumour resection, paired tagging was performed for
orientation purposes. Paired tagging consists of stitches marked with clips placed in the mucosa of both the surgical
cavity and the resection specimen on at least four corresponding anatomical locations. Stiches at matching
anatomical locations were marked with the same number of clips. Paired tagging ensured accurate relocation of the
anatomical site within the surgical cavity in case of an inadequate margin (Figure 1.1).16 In this study, in-vivo
imaging was not performed, since this results in inadequate illumination of the resection margins and therefore

Immediately after tumour excision, all sides of the resected specimen were imaged using a closed-field fluorescence

tissue slices by dedicated pathology staff. Next, images of all fresh tissue slices were acquired using the
fluorescence camera. Delineation of tumour tissue on fluorescence images was performed by two observers, based
on maximum fluorescence intensity and a substantial drop-off of signal towards all resection sides. From these
estimated tumour outlines, resection margins were measured on the images of the tissue slices, identifying the
closest margins based on fluorescence imaging. In case of disagreement between observers, a third observer was
consulted. If, based on fluorescence imaging, all margins were assessed as being tumour-free, FFS was performed
of the fresh tissue slice containing the estimated closest margin. When one or more inadequate margin(s) were
suspected based on fluorescence imaging of the fresh tissue slices, FFS of these margins was performed. In case
FFS confirmed an inadequate margin, the surgeon was informed by the pathologist. An additional resection was
performed if deemed clinically feasible and safe. Determining the exact location for additional resection was
essential for effective treatment. To ensure this, the following measures were taken: continuous orientation tracking
by two dedicated researchers throughout tissue imaging and processing, paired tagging to preserve anatomical
orientation, documentation of cutting planes during tissue slicing to enable accurate relocation of tissue slices in
the original resection specimen, and collaborative reporting by pathologist and researchers to the surgeon of the
precise location of any inadequate margins identified in the FFS. An exemption to this workflow was made only
for cases in which a tumour-positive margin was apparent based on visual and tactile assessment by both pathologist
and surgeon and fluorescence imaging of the fresh tissue slices. Even though not proven by FFS, an immediate
additional resection was performed. Altogether, two FG-FFS methods were investigated: 1) FFS of the tissue slice
identified by a spot and marked with a needle on whole resection specimen fluorescence imaging, and 2) FFS of
the tissue slice identified as the slice containing the closest margin by fresh tissue slice fluorescence imaging.
Following the FFS procedure, the fresh tissue slices were formalin fixed for at least 24h, followed by paraffin
embedding and 4 µm sectioning for H&E staining, according to standard of care. Based on the standard of care
H&E staining assessment, margins before and after potential additional resections were assessed by a pathologist.
Based on pathology results before and after study intervention, adjuvant treatment was determined by the
multidisciplinary head and neck tumour board of the UMCG. During the trial, adverse events were reported to the
Institutional Review Board using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 6.0.

Endpoints
In this study, three primary and two secondary endpoints were evaluated. The first primary endpoint was the
comparison between fluorescence imaging alone and FG-FFS for detecting tumour-positive and close surgical
margins. Diagnostic accuracy was evaluated by calculating sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, PPV and NPV for both
methods. An additional primary endpoint was the number of additional resections performed based on FG-FFS data
and the corresponding postoperative pathology outcomes. Tracer distribution, evaluated by correlating SBR values
of the whole resection specimen with margin widths, and conversely, margin widths with SBR values, was the last
primary endpoint of this study. The secondary endpoints were patient characteristics, feasibility of on-site
intraoperative tissue analysis by the surgeon and pathologist and feasibility of novel 3D imaging methods of the
obtained additional biopsies. Feasibility of novel 3D imaging methods of the obtained additional biopsies is not
reported here as it did not align with the primary focus of the trial. Feasibility of the analysis was assessed based
on duration of surgical procedures and integration of FG-FFS into the operative workflow.

Statistics & Reproducibility
The sample size was calculated using a two-proportion power analysis, assuming a baseline proportion of 0.5, an
expected proportion of 0.2, a 95% confidence level, 80% power, and resulted in a required sample size of at least
19 patients. Patients were excluded from the analysis in case they did not undergo all study procedures. The patients
were not randomised.
Descriptive statistics of patient demographics were tested using the Anderson-Darling test, D’Agostino & Pearson
test, Shapiro-Wilk test and Kolmogorov-Smirnov test using GraphPad Prism (version 9.0, GraphPad Software Inc,
San Diego, California, USA). Normally distributed data were reported using mean with standard deviation (SD)
and non-gaussian data using the median with interquartile range (IQR). Next, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, PPV
and NPV for margin assessment were calculated for both fluorescence imaging only and FG-FFS. Finally, FG-FFS
margin widths were compared with final pathology margins using a paired t-test and Bland-Altman analysis to
assess a potential bias. As this manuscript concerns a clinical intervention trial, all experiments could only be
performed once (during surgery).
